label: P.S. 236, Bronx
tag: Goal reachable but over budget; the city rates the roof not solar ready
question: How can our school cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget?

plan_summary.plain_answer: You asked how P.S. 236 can cut the electricity it buys from the grid by 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can be done, but only with the full package: deeper efficiency work, solar on the whole roof and a backup battery. That package is estimated to cut 31% to 46% of your 456,834 kWh a year, and it costs between $592,242 and $1,083,593 before credits, so it could run up to $283,593 over your budget. A smaller package of standard efficiency plus solar fits the budget and is estimated to cut 28% to 42%, so it could fall just short of 30%. Solar alone covers only about 22% to 24% of your use. You have no solar or efficiency work in place today, so the baseline is all grid electricity. The roof is 20 years or older and the city lists it as not solar ready, and no cost here includes roof repair or replacement. Next steps: get a structural engineer and a roofer to review the roof, and confirm your bills and the federal credit with the city agencies that approve school work. All figures are estimates with ranges.

# Professor Fritts — Priority roadmap

## In plain words

You asked how P.S. 236 can cut the electricity it buys from the grid by 30% by 2030 on an $800,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can be done, but only with the full package: deeper efficiency work, solar on the whole roof and a backup battery. That package is estimated to cut 31% to 46% of your 456,834 kWh a year, and it costs between $592,242 and $1,083,593 before credits, so it could run up to $283,593 over your budget. A smaller package of standard efficiency plus solar fits the budget and is estimated to cut 28% to 42%, so it could fall just short of 30%. Solar alone covers only about 22% to 24% of your use. You have no solar or efficiency work in place today, so the baseline is all grid electricity. The roof is 20 years or older and the city lists it as not solar ready, and no cost here includes roof repair or replacement. Next steps: get a structural engineer and a roofer to review the roof, and confirm your bills and the federal credit with the city agencies that approve school work. All figures are estimates with ranges.

## Who to contact and where to start

- [NYC Department of Education route: DCAS Energy Management](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dcas/agencies/energy-management.page): DCAS runs energy projects for city buildings; for a public school, start here before buying solar.
- [NYC School Construction Authority (SCA)](https://www.nycsca.org/): The SCA builds and repairs public school buildings, including roofs; roof work and solar on a school go through it.
- [NYC Public Schools](https://www.schools.nyc.gov/): The school system's facilities staff approve changes to a school building.
- [NYC Department of Buildings: Local Laws 92 and 94 (solar and green roofs)](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll92-solar-green-roofs.page): Replacing a roof triggers a rule to cover it with solar, a green roof, or both; plan the roof and solar together.
- [Con Edison: connecting solar to the grid](https://www.coned.com/en/save-money/using-distributed-generation-energy-sources/solar-energy/information-for-contractors): Every solar array needs a Con Edison interconnection application (a small or a large portal, depending on size). Contact: Con Edison Distributed Generation: dgexpert@coned.com.
- [Con Edison Solar Photovoltaics Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/solar-photovoltaics-guide.pdf): The utility's own steps, fees and timelines for connecting solar.
- [Con Edison Energy Storage System Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/specs-and-tariffs/energy-storage-guide.pdf): A battery has its own connection rules; this is the utility's guide for them.
- [NYC Department of Buildings](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/index.page): Permits for solar, batteries and roof work are filed here, by a registered design professional and a licensed electrician.
- [FDNY](https://www.nyc.gov/site/fdny/index.page): Rooftop solar and battery systems must meet FDNY access and safety rules.
- [NYSERDA NY-Sun](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/All-Programs/NY-Sun): The State's solar incentive program; confirm whether a public building can use it before counting any incentive.
- [NYC Accelerator](https://accelerator.nyc/): A city program that helps building owners with energy upgrades and compliance.

plan_summary.plain_answer: You asked how P.S. 38 can cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $600,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can, but not with efficiency work alone. Efficiency alone is estimated to cut only 6.2% to 17.6% of grid use, short of the goal. Efficiency plus a smaller rooftop solar array (about 114 kW) is estimated to cut 53.6% to 69.7%, at a typical upfront cost of $338,628 to $600,000, which fits your budget. The whole-roof array plus a backup battery could cover all of your use, but is estimated to cost $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget, so extending it is your decision. The school has no solar or efficiency work today. Limits: city records list the roof as not solar ready and 20 years or more old, and no cost here includes roof repair. The budget option gives no backup power in an outage. Heating fuel is outside this goal. Next steps: have a licensed engineer and a roofer review the roof, and confirm your bills and tariff.

# Professor Fritts — Priority roadmap

## In plain words

You asked how P.S. 38 can cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $600,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that it can, but not with efficiency work alone. Efficiency alone is estimated to cut only 6.2% to 17.6% of grid use, short of the goal. Efficiency plus a smaller rooftop solar array (about 114 kW) is estimated to cut 53.6% to 69.7%, at a typical upfront cost of $338,628 to $600,000, which fits your budget. The whole-roof array plus a backup battery could cover all of your use, but is estimated to cost $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget, so extending it is your decision. The school has no solar or efficiency work today. Limits: city records list the roof as not solar ready and 20 years or more old, and no cost here includes roof repair. The budget option gives no backup power in an outage. Heating fuel is outside this goal. Next steps: have a licensed engineer and a roofer review the roof, and confirm your bills and tariff.

## 1. Summary and goal status

- **FACT** (high): Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030, on a $600,000 capital budget set for 2027. The baseline is the 284,403 kWh (energy over time) the school buys from the grid each year. [284,403 kWh/yr] — source: `session://profile`
- **ESTIMATE** (low): Efficiency only is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual grid use. That does not reach the 30% goal, but it fits the budget. [6.2–17.6 % of annual use] — from the plan a costs and savings
- **ESTIMATE** (low): Efficiency plus a smaller solar array within budget is estimated to cut 53.6% to 69.7% of annual grid use. It reaches the goal even at the low end and fits the budget, if the roof can carry the array. [53.6–69.7 % of annual use] — from the plan b costs and savings
- **ESTIMATE** (low): The full path (deeper efficiency, whole-roof solar and a backup battery) is estimated to cover 100% of annual grid use but costs $473,046 to $1,119,287 more than your budget. Meeting the goal at full scale may take more than the amount set aside; whether to extend the budget is your decision once the gap is compared with the savings. [473,046–1,119,287 USD over budget] — from the plan c costs and savings
- **FACT** (medium): The goal is a percent cut in electricity, which is the kind of goal modeled here. — source: `session://profile`

## 2. Building profile and data provenance

question: Our rec center flooded in Hurricane Sandy and is used as a cooling center. How do we cut grid power 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages, on $750k?

intake.critical_loads: gym cooling, lighting and communications for a cooling center

plan_summary.plain_answer: You asked how to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages on $750,000. On paper the goal can be reached. A roof array sized to fit your budget is estimated to cut grid purchases by about 51% to 67%, at a typical cost of $418,771 to $750,000, but it gives no backup power in an outage. The full path adds deeper efficiency and a battery. It is estimated to cut 93% to 100% and cover about 8 to 9 hours of critical loads, but it costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is your decision once you compare that gap with the savings. The figures count electricity bought from the grid, and the 11.4 kW of solar already on the roof is treated as existing. The building sits in a mapped flood zone, is a landmark on parkland, and still needs structural and roof reviews. The battery size rests on an estimated load and an assumed 8 hours. Next, confirm your bills, critical-load figures and budget timing. Then commission the structural and roof reviews and ask for quotes with the battery and electrical gear placed above flood level.

claims.text: The goal is to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages, with a capital budget of $750,000 in budget year 2027.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only (Scenario A) is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual grid use, so it does not reach the 30% goal. It costs $65,824 to $226,165.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus a budget-capped solar array (Scenario B) is estimated to cut 50.8% to 66.6% of annual grid use and reaches the goal, within budget. It gives no backup power in an outage.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (Scenario C: deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 93.1% to 100% of annual grid use and covers about 8 to 9.4 hours of critical loads. It costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Meeting both the 30% goal and outage backup may take more than $750,000. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision once the gap is compared with the estimated savings.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Red Hook Recreation Center (NYC Parks) at 155 Bay Street, Brooklyn is a flat-roofed park recreation center built in 1936 with 27,069 sq ft of floor area and a roof area of 32,860 sq ft, as entered by the user. The utility is Con Edison.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Annual grid electricity of 375,066 kWh (kWh is energy over time) is the working baseline. It matches the city's 2024 building energy report (375,066 kWh). The goal baseline is electricity bought from the grid, which the existing solar already lowers.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Existing solar of 11.4 kW (kW is how much power at one moment) is already on the roof and is taken into account. The city's roof-solar record lists it with estimated output of 12,540 kWh a year.

claims.text: The plan assumes no other existing efficiency work or renewables, because none were reported. Lighting type, controls and cooling type were not given. Efficiency work already done would lower the savings below.

# Professor Fritts — Priority roadmap

## In plain words

You asked how to cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep critical loads running in outages on $750,000. On paper the goal can be reached. A roof array sized to fit your budget is estimated to cut grid purchases by about 51% to 67%, at a typical cost of $418,771 to $750,000, but it gives no backup power in an outage. The full path adds deeper efficiency and a battery. It is estimated to cut 93% to 100% and cover about 8 to 9 hours of critical loads, but it costs $134,342 to $728,885 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is your decision once you compare that gap with the savings. The figures count electricity bought from the grid, and the 11.4 kW of solar already on the roof is treated as existing. The building sits in a mapped flood zone, is a landmark on parkland, and still needs structural and roof reviews. The battery size rests on an estimated load and an assumed 8 hours. Next, confirm your bills, critical-load figures and budget timing. Then commission the structural and roof reviews and ask for quotes with the battery and electrical gear placed above flood level.

## 1. Summary and goal status

- **ESTIMATE** (medium): The full path (Scenario C: deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 93.1% to 100% of annual grid use and covers about 8 to 9.4 hours of critical loads. question: Our library is in the Greenwich Village Historic District. Can we put solar on the roof, and how do we cut grid power 30% by 2030 on $500k?

plan_summary.plain_answer: You asked whether the library can have rooftop solar and how to cut grid power 30% by 2030 on $500,000. Solar cannot be sized yet. The roof is pitched, and the planning rules do not allow solar to be sized on a pitched roof until an engineer or roofer verifies the usable area. This was a decision from those rules, not missing data. The building is also a city landmark, so a Landmarks Preservation Commission review is needed before any rooftop work, and the city's roof assessment lists the roof as not solar ready. An efficiency package alone is estimated to cut grid use by about 6% to 18% of your 268,331 kWh a year. That falls short of 30%, and it costs an estimated $47,092 to $161,804, well inside your budget. The plan assumes no existing solar or efficiency work. The gas heating is outside an electricity goal. Next steps: have an engineer or roofer verify the usable roof area, and start the landmarks and structural reviews. Then re-run the plan to compare solar and battery options against the 30% goal.

# Professor Fritts — Priority roadmap

## In plain words

You asked whether the library can have rooftop solar and how to cut grid power 30% by 2030 on $500,000. Solar cannot be sized yet. The roof is pitched, and the planning rules do not allow solar to be sized on a pitched roof until an engineer or roofer verifies the usable area. This was a decision from those rules, not missing data. The building is also a city landmark, so a Landmarks Preservation Commission review is needed before any rooftop work, and the city's roof assessment lists the roof as not solar ready. An efficiency package alone is estimated to cut grid use by about 6% to 18% of your 268,331 kWh a year. That falls short of 30%, and it costs an estimated $47,092 to $161,804, well inside your budget. The plan assumes no existing solar or efficiency work. The gas heating is outside an electricity goal. Next steps: have an engineer or roofer verify the usable roof area, and start the landmarks and structural reviews. Then re-run the plan to compare solar and battery options against the 30% goal.

- [FDNY](https://www.nyc.gov/site/fdny/index.page): Rooftop solar and battery systems must meet FDNY access and safety rules.
- [NYSERDA NY-Sun](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/All-Programs/NY-Sun): The State's solar incentive program; confirm whether a public building can use it before counting any incentive.
- [NYC Accelerator](https://accelerator.nyc/): A city program that helps building owners with energy upgrades and compliance.

incentives.name: Federal elective pay (direct pay) for governmental entities, solar investment credit (IRC 6417 / 48E)
incentives.status_note: Governmental entities can receive the credit as a direct payment. Solar property must be placed in service by 2027-12-31 (26 U.S.C. 48E(e)(4)(A), for facilities whose construction begins after 2026-07-04). Whether a particular school or agency qualifies is not confirmed here.
incentives.quote: Tax-exempt and governmental entities can benefit from certain clean energy investment and production credits using new options enabled by legislation enacted in 2022.

incentives.name: NYC Solar Schools program (DCAS, NYPA, NYC Public Schools): rooftop solar on DOE schools under power purchase agreements
incentives.status_note: Ongoing: 130 installations done and more in progress per the city's release. The release describes no enrollment process, and it is not known whether this building is in the pipeline. Ask DCAS or the SCA.
incentives.quote: To date, DCAS and NYCPS have completed 130 solar installations on public schools, totaling 27.5 megawatts of added renewable power to the city’s portfolio, building on the city’s larger decarbonization efforts.

incentives.name: NYC Local Laws 92 and 94 of 2019 (sustainable roofs): rule, not an incentive
incentives.status_note: Applies to new buildings and existing buildings undergoing certain major roof renovations: the roof must have a solar photovoltaic system, a green roof system, or both, over any applicable roof.
incentives.quote: It is a huge step forward that all new buildings will have either a solar photovoltaic or green roof system.

claims.text: Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget (budget year 2027), for P.S. 24 at 660 West 236 Street, Bronx.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Efficiency only is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, which is 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal and fits the budget.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Efficiency plus solar within budget is estimated to cut 43% to 58% of annual use, which is 143% to 193% of the goal. It reaches the goal at the low end and fits the budget, with the high-cost case at the budget limit.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The full path (deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 66.6% to 84.9% of annual use and reaches the goal, but costs $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision after comparing that gap with the savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Every figure in this plan is a planning estimate with a range; no savings figure is certain.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: P.S. 24 is a flat-roofed elementary school built in 1953, with 115,325 sq ft of floor area and a 40,500 sq ft roof as entered by the user. The owning agency is the Department of Education.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Existing solar already on the roof: 228.2 kW. The city's solar readiness record also lists 228.2 kW installed, financed through a power purchase agreement (PPA), with estimated production of 249,879 kWh a year. No other existing renewables or efficiency work were reported, so the plan assumes none.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Annual grid use is 226,605 kWh. This is electricity bought from the grid, after the existing array. It matches the city's Local Law 84 energy report for 2024, which also shows an energy use per square foot (EUI) of 48.4 kBtu (thousand BTU).
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city report also shows natural gas use of about 4,353,100 kBtu, so heating appears to run on gas. Gas heating is outside an electricity-use goal and is not counted here.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Building footprints on the tax lot total about 40,497 sq ft across two buildings, close to the roof area the user entered. A footprint is ground area, not a measured roof.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: The city record shows no landmark flag.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: Solar output range: system losses of 18% (low) to 10% (high) around the standard 14% default; weather is typical-year data.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Usable roof is 55% of the roof area after setbacks.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Panel density is 66 sq ft per kW DC.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Critical load was not given, so it is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft, or 115.3 kW (not metered). Backup length was not given, so 8 hours is assumed. Battery energy is 1,085 kWh after round-trip losses.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Efficiency measures (LED and controls) save 10-20% of annual use. This is a planning estimate, not a cited benchmark and not a building model.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: Prices are planning-level benchmarks, not quotes, from NYSERDA data on completed NYC projects. Only 62% to 88% of predicted efficiency savings is counted, because the City's audited projects delivered that share (Local Law 87 report, DCAS, FY2022). The deep-efficiency saving of 15-25% is also a planning estimate.
claims.label: ASSUMPTION

claims.text: The baseline for the goal is the 226,605 kWh the building buys from the grid each year. The existing solar array already lowers this figure, so the 30% cut is measured against what is left.
claims.label: FACT

claims.text: A standard efficiency package (LED and controls) is estimated to cut 14,050 to 39,882 kWh a year. Only 62% to 88% of predicted savings is counted, since the City's audited projects delivered that share. Whether LED lighting is already installed is unknown; any lighting already upgraded would lower these savings.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The roof area entered gives about 22,275 sq ft of usable roof after setbacks, which would hold about 337.5 kW if the roof were empty.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The roof rules do not allow a second whole-roof array on top of the existing 228.2 kW array. Only about 109 kW of free roof is left. This is a decision from the roof rules, not missing data. The first request for 337.5 kW was declined for that reason and the 109 kW size was used instead.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: A new 109 kW array is estimated to produce 129,802 to 142,640 kWh a year (about 136,223 kWh typical), using flat-roof tilt and typical-year weather.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The new array alone is about 60% of annual grid use. Surplus solar is zero, so nothing flows to the grid uncredited.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Electricity price is a New York commercial average of $0.1981 to $0.2418 per kWh ($0.222 typical), not this building's own tariff. Annual savings from the new array are estimated at $25,714 to $34,490 (about $30,242 typical).
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: The city's solar readiness record gives no roof condition or roof age, and the year the roof was last replaced was not provided. Roof area, condition and age should be verified by an engineer or roofer.
claims.label: RECOMMENDATION

claims.text: Scenario A, efficiency only: reduces 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use (21% to 59% of the goal). Upfront $39,769 to $136,643; net cost the same; simple payback 4.1 to 49.1 years; within budget (14% to 34% of it); no outage backup. Does not reach the goal.
claims.label: ESTIMATE

claims.text: Scenario B, efficiency plus 70.2 kW of new solar: reduces 43% to 58% of annual use (143% to 193% of the goal). Upfront $217,212 to $400,000; net cost $163,979 to $320,993; simple payback 5.2 to 16.6 years; within budget (54% to 100% of it); no outage backup. Reaches the goal.

# Professor Fritts — Priority roadmap

## In plain words

You asked how to cut grid electricity another 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget. The plan estimates the goal can be reached within budget. Efficiency plus a new array on the free part of the roof is estimated to cut grid use by about 43% to 58%, for a typical cost range of $217,212 to $400,000. Efficiency alone is estimated to reach only 6% to 18%, so it falls short. The building already has a 228 kW solar array, and the 226,605 kWh figure is electricity bought from the grid after that array. Only about 109 kW of roof is still free, so this was a decision from the roof rules, not missing data. The full path with a backup battery is estimated at $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget, and the first two options give no outage backup. Next, have a structural engineer and roofer confirm the roof area and condition, and ask the city school agencies whether this building is already in line for more solar.

## 1. Summary and goal status

- **FACT** (high): Goal: cut electricity bought from the grid by 30% by 2030 on a $400,000 capital budget (budget year 2027), for P.S. 24 at 660 West 236 Street, Bronx. [30 % of annual grid use] — source: `session://profile`
- **ESTIMATE** (medium): Efficiency only is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of annual use, which is 21% to 59% of the goal. It does not reach the goal and fits the budget. [6.2–17.6 % of annual use] — from the plan a costs and savings
- **ESTIMATE** (medium): Efficiency plus solar within budget is estimated to cut 43% to 58% of annual use, which is 143% to 193% of the goal. It reaches the goal at the low end and fits the budget, with the high-cost case at the budget limit. [43–58 % of annual use] — from the plan b costs and savings
- **ESTIMATE** (medium): The full path (deeper efficiency, the whole free roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 66.6% to 84.9% of annual use and reaches the goal, but costs $518,120 to $1,064,693 more than your budget. Whether to extend the budget is the owner's decision after comparing that gap with the savings. [518,120–1,064,693 USD above budget] — from the plan c costs and savings
- **RECOMMENDATION** (high): Every figure in this plan is a planning estimate with a range; no savings figure is certain. — from the plan b costs and savings

## 2. Building profile and data provenance

- **FACT** (medium): Existing solar already on the roof: 228.2 kW. ## Who to contact and where to start

- [NYC Department of Education route: DCAS Energy Management](https://www.nyc.gov/site/dcas/agencies/energy-management.page): DCAS runs energy projects for city buildings; for a public school, start here before buying solar.
- [NYC School Construction Authority (SCA)](https://www.nycsca.org/): The SCA builds and repairs public school buildings, including roofs; roof work and solar on a school go through it.
- [NYC Public Schools](https://www.schools.nyc.gov/): The school system's facilities staff approve changes to a school building.
- [Con Edison: connecting solar to the grid](https://www.coned.com/en/save-money/using-distributed-generation-energy-sources/solar-energy/information-for-contractors): Every solar array needs a Con Edison interconnection application (a small or a large portal, depending on size). Contact: Con Edison Distributed Generation: dgexpert@coned.com.
- [Con Edison Solar Photovoltaics Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/solar-photovoltaics-guide.pdf): The utility's own steps, fees and timelines for connecting solar.
- [Con Edison Energy Storage System Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/specs-and-tariffs/energy-storage-guide.pdf): A battery has its own connection rules; this is the utility's guide for them.
- [NYC Department of Buildings](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/index.page): Permits for solar, batteries and roof work are filed here, by a registered design professional and a licensed electrician.
- [FDNY](https://www.nyc.gov/site/fdny/index.page): Rooftop solar and battery systems must meet FDNY access and safety rules.
- [NYSERDA NY-Sun](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/All-Programs/NY-Sun): The State's solar incentive program; confirm whether a public building can use it before counting any incentive.
- [NYC Accelerator](https://accelerator.nyc/): A city program that helps building owners with energy upgrades and compliance.

label: Flushing Library, Queens
tag: Close to the goal only with the full path, which runs over budget; the roof is poor and 20+ years old
question: Our branch library is a cooling center during heat waves. How do we cut grid power 30% by 2030 and keep the cooling running in outages, on $1.5M?

intake.critical_loads: cooling and lighting for a cooling center during outages

plan_summary.plain_answer: You asked how the Flushing Library can cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep its cooling running in outages on a $1,500,000 capital budget. The plan estimates that none of the three paths clearly reaches 30%. Efficiency alone is estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of the 2,241,970 kWh a year the library buys from the grid, and adding a solar array that fits the budget raises that to 8.3% to 19.9%. The full path (deeper efficiency, solar on the whole roof and a backup battery) is estimated to cut 17.0% to 30.4%, so it reaches 30% only at the top of its range, and it costs up to $1,345,721 more than your budget. Rooftop solar alone covers only about 7.7% to 8.4% of your use, because the building is large and the roof is small. The city rates the roof Poor, not solar ready and 20 years or more old, and none of the costs include repairing or replacing it. Next: have an engineer and a roofer review the roof, then book an energy audit before deciding whether to extend the budget.

outcome.label: Not within budget
outcome.headline: Not on your $1,500,000 budget. Within it, the best plan (Plan B) cuts grid use 8.3-19.9%. The full path reaches 30% only at its best, and could cost up to $1.35M more.
outcome.subhead: Plan C cuts grid use 17-30.4%, so the goal is met only if savings land at the high end.

You asked how the Flushing Library can cut grid electricity 30% by 2030 and keep its cooling running in outages on a $1,500,000 capital budget. Rooftop solar alone covers only about 7.7% to 8.4% of your use, because the building is large and the roof is small. The city rates the roof Poor, not solar ready and 20 years or more old, and none of the costs include repairing or replacing it. ## 8. Priority roadmap

- **RECOMMENDATION** (medium): Phase 0, confirm data and budget: gather 12 months of Con Edison bills, confirm the capital budget year (2027) and that $1,500,000 is a one-time total, and confirm the tariff on a bill. Confirm the roof area and the year the roof was last replaced. — from the plan b costs and savings
- **RECOMMENDATION** (high): Phase 1, professional reviews: a licensed structural engineer (PE) or registered architect (RA) analysis of the roof, plus a roof condition survey and a roofer's quote for repair or replacement. The roof cannot be certified from these records. — [source](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Solar-Readiness-Assessments-Local-Law-24/cfz5-6fvh)
- **RECOMMENDATION** (low): Phase 2, efficiency measures: an energy audit, then LED lighting, building controls and other measures as confirmed by the audit, which are estimated to cut 6.2% to 17.6% of grid use. — from the plan a costs and savings
- **RECOMMENDATION** (medium): Phase 3, permits and interconnection: Department of Buildings permits, a licensed electrician, FDNY rooftop access review, and the Con Edison interconnection application. Confirm the approval route with the Queens Public Library system. — from the plan b costs and savings
- **RECOMMENDATION** (low): Phase 4, solar installation: only after the roof is repaired or replaced. The array that fits the budget is about 39.5 kW; the whole roof could hold about 146 kW. Place the solar in service before 2027-12-31 if the federal direct payment is to be pursued. — from the plan b costs and savings
- **RECOMMENDATION** (low): Phase 5, battery, commissioning and verification: add the backup battery if backup for cooling and lighting during outages is wanted, then check results against 12 months of bills. — from the plan c costs and savings

## 9. Resilience and reliability plan

- **ESTIMATE** (low): Scenario C is estimated to carry the critical loads for 8 to 9.4 hours in an outage. The critical loads are cooling and lighting for the library's use as a cooling center. [8–9.4 hours] — from the plan c costs and savings
- **ESTIMATE** (medium): Scenarios A and B give no backup power. Solar panels shut off in an outage without a battery. — from the plan b costs and savings
- **ASSUMPTION** (low): Battery sizing of 76.0 kW and 715 kWh is a planning estimate, because the critical load and backup hours were not given: the load is estimated at 1.0 W per sq ft and 8 hours is assumed. A metered critical load would change the size.
- **FACT** (medium): The FEMA effective map shows minimal flood hazard (zone X), so no flood-zone review is triggered. Only the flood zone was read. — [source](https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28)

## Who to contact and where to start

- [NYC Department of Buildings: Local Laws 92 and 94 (solar and green roofs)](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll92-solar-green-roofs.page): Replacing a roof triggers a rule to cover it with solar, a green roof, or both; plan the roof and solar together.
- [Con Edison: connecting solar to the grid](https://www.coned.com/en/save-money/using-distributed-generation-energy-sources/solar-energy/information-for-contractors): Every solar array needs a Con Edison interconnection application (a small or a large portal, depending on size). Contact: Con Edison Distributed Generation: dgexpert@coned.com.
- [Con Edison Solar Photovoltaics Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/solar-photovoltaics-guide.pdf): The utility's own steps, fees and timelines for connecting solar.
- [Con Edison Energy Storage System Guide (PDF)](https://www.coned.com/-/media/files/coned/documents/save-energy-money/using-private-generation/specs-and-tariffs/energy-storage-guide.pdf): A battery has its own connection rules; this is the utility's guide for them.
- [NYC Department of Buildings](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/index.page): Permits for solar, batteries and roof work are filed here, by a registered design professional and a licensed electrician.
- [FDNY](https://www.nyc.gov/site/fdny/index.page): Rooftop solar and battery systems must meet FDNY access and safety rules.
- [NYSERDA NY-Sun](https://www.nyserda.ny.gov/All-Programs/NY-Sun): The State's solar incentive program; confirm whether a public building can use it before counting any incentive.
- [NYC Accelerator](https://accelerator.nyc/): A city program that helps building owners with energy upgrades and compliance.
